title: External identification and electrothermal modeling of persistent-current-switch operating states in a Siemens MRI magnet
abstract: A persistent current switch (PCS) closes the superconducting loop of an MRI magnet; a heater makes it resistive so an external supply can change the magnet current. PCS control is usually treated as binary: heater on--resistive, heater off--superconducting. External current and voltage logs from an MPS2 service power supply (Digit Systems) show for a Siemens MAGNETOM Avanto magnet that the command does not uniquely determine the PCS state: after heater switch-off, Joule self-heating can sustain the resistive state. Purpose-designed maneuvers separate two resistive regimes. With the heater energized, the branch resistance is nearly constant at 1.86--2.19 $Ω$ below 0.5 V. After switch-off, the self-sustained regime follows $R_{sw}=0.65|V_{node}|^{1.5}$ ($R_{sw}$ in ohms, $V_{node}$ in volts) and is 12-fold below the heater-on resistance at 0.4 V. Both regimes obey one electrothermal relation, $R_{sw}=C(P_h h+V_{node}^2/R_{sw})^a$, with $h$ the binary heater command, over a 690-fold resistance range. First, branch resistance and coil inductance set the redistribution time constant, $τ=L/R_{sw}$; final-hold duration therefore controls persistent-current accuracy. Across 18 service sessions on other Siemens magnets, analyzed without transferring the Avanto coefficients, the median hold was $13τ$ and the median residual branch current was 8 ppm of coil current. Second, the intersection of the PCS characteristic and external-circuit load line sets the self-sustainment boundary. The cross-session estimate of 0.062 V lies between observed retrapping at 0.06 V and retention at 0.07 V. In dynamic simulation, the two fixed-coefficient characteristics $R(V,h)$ reduce current RMSE from 1.449 to 0.154 A (9.4-fold); omitting explicit heater input gives no improvement over the inductance-only model.
summary: This paper develops a detailed electrothermal model for a Persistent Current Switch (PCS) in an MRI magnet, moving beyond simple on/off control. By analyzing external voltage and current logs, the authors quantify how Joule self-heating sustains resistive states after the heater is turned off. The resulting model significantly improves the accuracy of dynamic simulations describing the complex switching behavior.
main_problem: To move beyond treating Persistent Current Switch (PCS) control as purely binary, the authors quantitatively model its operating states by accounting for Joule self-heating effects after heater deactivation.
main_result: The proposed electrothermal model successfully describes both resistive regimes using a unified relation, significantly improving dynamic simulation accuracy compared to simpler models.
method: The study combines external electrical measurements from service sessions with detailed electrothermal modeling and dynamic simulations.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting MRI magnet containing a PCS connected in parallel with the main coil. The model treats the PCS resistance as dependent on both node voltage and heater command, governed by an electrothermal balance equation.
key_observables: Branch resistance ($R_{sw}$), self-sustainment boundary voltage ($\approx 0.062	ext{ V}$), current Root Mean Square Error (RMSE).
important_parameters: Inductance ($L$), time constant ($	au = L/R_{sw}$), heater command ($h$), and the electrothermal relation coefficients ($C, a$).
main_assumptions: The model parameters are specific to the tested Siemens Avanto unit and do not automatically transfer to other magnets or full operating currents.
figures_summary: Not specified (Analysis relies on logs of current/voltage over time).
paper_structure: The paper analyzes external electrical measurements from service sessions, develops a unified electrothermal model linking two distinct resistive regimes (heater-on vs. self-sustained), and validates the model using dynamic simulations.
why_interesting: While focused on classical superconducting magnet engineering, the underlying principle of modeling hysteretic, non-linear, history-dependent electrical switching behavior is relevant to understanding quantum circuit switches or Josephson junction dynamics where state transitions are critical.

Figure 4: Initiating ̸= sustaining: the same 0.10 V setpoint sustains an existing resistive state but does not re-create it after a four-second reset. After the setpoint returns, the node voltage stays near zero and the supply current reaches the limit. The bottom lane is the CAN heater command (1 — on, 0 — off): both compared episodes run at h = 0; the heater is switched on again only at the end of the window.

Figure 5: Seven pulses at a 0.5 V setpoint with the heater on continuously. The settled pulses are annotated with the resistance from the trailing-edge technique (Section 4.1): 2.08–2.15 Ω at heater operating times of 109–819 s. No systematic trend with duration is visible; the full resistance range is 3.3 %, and the branch current changes by less than 1 %. The first pulse preceded the long zero pause needed for the independent determination of the coil current and is excluded from the statistics. The bottom lane is the CAN heater command, which stays on throughout the series.
